summaries.example: Imagine a stone on a beach. If you pick it up and use it as a paperweight, you are using a natural thing for a job, but you may not have made an artifact. If you shape the stone into a tool for cracking nuts, it is a clearer example of an artifact because you changed it on purpose for a purpose. Even this example raises questions: how much changing is enough?
summaries.summary: Artifacts are things people make or change for purposes. A chair, spoon, house, or tool seems to fit this idea. But the borders are not easy to draw. A path might form because people walk over the same ground many times, without anyone planning it. A natural stone can be used as a hammer even if nobody shaped it. A made object can also have several uses, including uses its maker never imagined. The entry asks whether “artifact” names a clear kind of thing or whether nature and human making blend into a long series of cases. It also asks whether artifacts really exist, what makes kinds such as “chair” or “book” real, and how functions are connected to makers, users, physical parts, and histories of copying. Some artifacts are not ordinary objects: a musical work, piece of software, or institution may be created and changed without being located in one place. Finally, artifacts do not merely serve our purposes. Lists, tools, spaces, and other objects can support memory, guide action, and influence how people think.
key_ideas: A common definition says an artifact is made intentionally, changes some material, and has a purpose.
This definition has blurry edges. A path, shell, or stone may be natural, made, used, or changed in ways that do not fit neatly into one box.
Philosophers disagree about whether artifacts truly exist, what makes artifact kinds real, and how objects get their functions.
Some artifacts, such as songs, software, or institutions, may not be ordinary solid objects.
Things we make can also help shape how we think, remember, work, and act.
summaries.why_it_matters: We live among artifacts all the time, from phones and clothes to roads and buildings. Thinking carefully about them helps us understand how human purposes, materials, habits, and culture fit together. It also shows that the things around us can shape our thinking and behavior, not just help us carry out plans.

important_terms.definition: Something made or changed on purpose to do a job or reach a goal. Philosophers often use this word more strictly than people do in everyday speech.
The job something is meant to do or can do. A spoon’s function may be helping us eat, but people can also use it for other jobs.
Things that happen or exist without being made by people, such as stars, trees, or a naturally formed stone.
A big philosophical question about what kinds of things are really part of the world and in what way they exist.
A thing that happens again and again, such as many copies of a book or many performances of a song.

questions_to_think_about: Is a shell used as a paperweight an artifact, a natural object, or both in different ways?
Can something have a function even when it does not work?
Is a song the same thing as one performance of the song?
How do notebooks, maps, or lists help people think?

summaries.example: Consider a standard traffic sign. One view says it exists as an artifact because a person with the relevant knowledge intentionally produced a piece of metal and paint to perform a recognized function. A different view emphasizes the role of social conventions and language in making it a sign. A cosmic event that happened to create the same pattern would not seem to produce a traffic sign. Yet the case also illustrates a larger issue: an artifact depends on physical materials, human intentions, and social practices, while those practices are themselves part of the natural world.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of artifacts begins with a familiar proposal: an artifact is intentionally made, materially modified, and produced for a purpose. The proposal distinguishes artifacts from naturally occurring objects and from accidental by-products. However, each condition admits borderline cases. Repeated travel can create a path without a designing intention; a found shell or stone can serve a purpose without modification; and biological and cultural functions can overlap in domesticated organisms. These cases motivate the continuum problem: nature and artifact may be connected by gradual transitions rather than separated by a metaphysical boundary. Some philosophers introduce intermediate categories, while others argue that “artifact” is not a useful theoretical category for anthropology, archaeology, or environmental philosophy. The metaphysics of artifacts then asks whether ordinary objects exist at all, whether artifacts are intention-dependent, and whether wholes are more than their material parts. Proposed answers include eliminativism, constitution theories, and accounts tied to the conditions under which our terms successfully apply. Related disputes concern artifact kinds: they may be copied forms with histories, kinds constituted partly by makers’ intentions, or categories valuable because they support inference and explanation. Function is equally contested. A function may arise from intention, social acceptance, a history of reproduction, or a system’s causal organization. These theories must address nonstandard uses, malfunction, novel prototypes, and “phantom” functions that objects cannot actually perform. key_ideas: The standard definition uses intention, material modification, and purpose, but paths, residues, domesticated organisms, and naturally found tools create borderline cases.

The continuum problem suggests that nature and culture may not divide into two sharply separated realms. Some philosophers respond with intermediate categories; others question whether “artifact” is methodologically useful at all.
Debates about existence include eliminativist views, constitution views, and approaches that connect the existence of ordinary objects with the application conditions of our terms.
Artifact kinds may be understood as mind-independent copied kinds, as intention-dependent kinds, or as groupings useful for human inquiry without requiring fixed essences.
Theories of function range from strongly intentional accounts to views emphasizing reproduction histories, causal roles, social practices, or mixtures of these factors.

Repeatable artworks and other named products raise the problem of abstract artifacts: how can something outside space and time be created, changed, or destroyed? Artifacts also participate in cognition by scaffolding memory, planning, and action.
summaries.why_it_matters: Artifacts occupy the meeting point of ontology, technology, culture, language, psychology, and action. Clarifying them can affect how we understand design, engineering, archaeology, art, environmental restoration, and social institutions. The discussion also challenges the idea that human minds simply impose order on a passive world: objects and built environments can organize memory, constrain behavior, and help constitute cognitive activity.

important_terms.definition: In the standard philosophical account, an object intentionally produced, involving material modification, for some purpose. The entry examines whether these conditions form a sharp boundary.
The area of metaphysics concerned with what exists and how existing things are structured or depend on one another.
The view that ordinary objects, including some artifacts, do not exist in the robust sense claimed by common thought.
The philosophical study of parts and wholes, including the question of when parts compose a unified object.
A way of classifying things made for human purposes, such as books, chairs, software, or paintings; philosophers debate whether these kinds are mind-dependent.
An account of function that treats a feature’s role in a system as important, rather than relying only on a designer’s intention.
An artifact that is not located in ordinary space and time but is intentionally created and can have multiple instances, such as a musical work on some theories.
The proposal that cognitive activity can be distributed across brains, bodies, people, and environmental objects rather than occurring only inside an individual brain.

questions_to_think_about: Does a sharp philosophical boundary between natural objects and artifacts help inquiry, or can it distort the phenomena being studied?
What conditions would make a collection of parts a genuine artifact rather than merely material arranged in a certain way?
Should an unsuccessful prototype have a function? What about an object made for a purpose that cannot possibly achieve it?
Are artifact kinds real because makers intend them, because successful forms are copied, or because the categories support explanation and practice?
If a notebook performs a memory task outside the brain, is it part of the cognitive process or merely a tool used by that process?

summaries.example: Suppose students keep walking across a grassy field between the school and a bus stop. Over time, a path appears. Nobody planned it, but people use it for a purpose. Now imagine the school deliberately clears and maintains the same path. Is the second path an artifact while the first is not? Or are they both part of material culture, even though only one fits the strict philosophical definition? The example shows why classifying objects can depend on what we are trying to understand.
summaries.summary: Artifacts seem to be everywhere: tools, buildings, clothes, software, artworks, and systems of social practice. A standard philosophical account says that an artifact is intentionally produced, involves material modification, and is made for a purpose. This definition separates artifacts from natural objects, accidental leftovers, and natural objects merely put to use. Yet the separation becomes difficult in borderline cases. Paths may form unintentionally, a stone may be used as a hammer without being shaped, and domesticated plants and animals can have both biological and cultural roles. These examples create a continuum between nature and human making. Some thinkers propose categories between nature and artifact, while others prefer the broader idea of material culture or question whether “artifact” helps researchers understand human life. Metaphysics adds further disputes. Some philosophers deny that many ordinary objects exist in the fullest sense; others argue that artifacts exist because materials can constitute new objects under the right intentions, conventions, and circumstances. Artifact kinds—such as chair, book, or tool—may depend on copying histories, makers’ concepts, design features, or practical and explanatory interests. Function is also debated. A function can be linked to intention, repeated production, causal contribution, or social acceptance. These theories must explain unusual uses, broken objects, new prototypes, and objects believed to work even when they do not. The idea of abstract artifacts extends the discussion to musical works, software, and other repeatable things that are created but are not single physical objects. key_ideas: The strict definition of artifact requires intentional making, material change, and purpose, but real cases often fall between categories.
A natural object used as a tool may be called a naturefact in one philosophical classification, while modified but unintended leftovers may be treated as a separate kind of residue.
Philosophers disagree about whether artifacts are fully real, partly dependent on human intentions, or best understood through the way our concepts work.
Artifact kinds are not necessarily like biological kinds. Their identity may involve design, copying, social practices, visible structure, and rules about proper use.
An object’s function may come from a maker’s intention, a history of successful copying, its role in a system, or a combination of these factors.
Objects such as notebooks, maps, and the arrangement of items on a counter can help organize thinking and behavior.
summaries.why_it_matters: Understanding artifacts helps explain the human-made world without assuming that every case is simple. It connects everyday questions about tools and objects with larger issues about reality, language, culture, technology, and thinking. It also reminds us that tools and environments can influence our habits and ideas.

important_terms.definition: Usually, something intentionally made or changed from materials in order to serve a purpose. Philosophers debate whether this definition is too narrow.
The intended or actual job of an object, such as a phone’s communication function or a chair’s sitting function.
The idea that cases form a gradual range rather than falling into two sharply separated groups.
A group or category of objects, such as chairs, books, or tools, whose reality and membership philosophers try to explain.
The study of what exists, including questions about ordinary objects, parts, wholes, and dependence.
The view that some ordinary objects may not really exist, even though ordinary language treats them as real.
An object or work that is not located in space and time in the same way as a physical chair, but is intentionally created and may have copies or performances.
The idea that thinking can depend on organized activity involving people, bodies, tools, and surroundings.

questions_to_think_about: Would a naturally formed path become an artifact if people started maintaining it? Why?
Can an object have more than one function? Which function counts as its proper one?
If a chair is used as a plant stand, is it still a chair?
Why might a musical work be different from one performance of it?
How might the layout of a classroom change what students do?
